screens.title: Deploying a Substrate Node to the Cloud
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to take a compiled Substrate node into the cloud and run it reliably. We'll cover the decisions that matter when choosing a provider and instance type, how to prepare a Linux server with secure access, why you should use a service manager rather than a terminal session, and what monitoring looks like for an operational node. You will see concrete command examples for an Ubuntu system, a defensible firewall setup, a persistent service file using the system's service manager, and options for telemetry and external monitoring. Knowing these steps matters because nodes need persistent connectivity, reliable restarts, and careful network controls to participate in a peer-to-peer blockchain safely. For example, a full node can run on a modest virtual machine with SSD storage while a validator requires greater availability and more powerful hardware. Keep a mental checklist: choose the right instance, lock down SSH, open only required ports, build in a persistent data path, run under systemd, and attach telemetry. As you proceed, ask: is my node resilient to reboots and restricted to the traffic I expect?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Deploying a Substrate Node
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Deploying a Substrate Node to the Cloud

Turn a compiled node into a resilient cloud service: instance selection, Linux setup, firewall rules, systemd service, and monitoring.

In this lesson
  • Choose provider and instance type suitable for full or validator nodes.
  • Prepare a secure Ubuntu/Debian server with SSH keys and firewall rules.
  • Build the node and run it as a persistent systemd service with monitoring.
Why it matters

Nodes must be resilient to reboots and network changes. Proper deployment ensures uptime, predictable logs, and secure RPC access for your dApp clients.

Visual overview
Instance
Pick CPU, RAM, SSD sized for chain growth and role.
Server Setup
SSH keys, user, dependencies, build tools.
Service
systemd for restarts, logs, and startup ordering.
Explore Key Topics
Choosing Instance Types
Match CPU, RAM, and SSD to node role. Always overprovision disk space.
Server Hardening
SSH keys, non-root user, UFW rules to protect RPC and WS.
systemd & Monitoring
Run the node as a service, integrate telemetry, and consider Prometheus/Grafana for metrics.
This hero slide orients you to the chapter. Proceed to learn objective pages that define the measurable outcomes for a successful deployment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to practical skills you'll use when deploying a Substrate node. First, you will learn to select an appropriate cloud provider and instance type by matching C P U, R A M, and SSD needs to the node role. For a full node that serves peers, modest virtual machines with solid-state storage are sufficient; for a validator you will place emphasis on availability and stronger hardware. Second, you will configure a Linux server environment: connect over SSH, update packages, and install the build dependencies required to compile a Substrate node. Third, you will implement secure SSH access and basic server hardening: use key-based authentication, create a non-root user, disable direct root login, and apply firewall rules that open only the P2P port broadly while restricting RPC and WebSocket to trusted IPs. Finally, you will set up the node as a persistent systemd service and monitor its health using journal logs and telemetry. Each objective is actionable and verifiable, so you'll be ready to run a resilient node in production.

screens.title: Objectives — Deployment Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: This page turns objectives into a short checklist you can follow during deployment. Start by choosing a cloud provider and instance that fits your node role. If you run a simple full node, a small instance with solid-state drive and 4 gigabytes of memory often suffices; for validators prefer higher availability and more C P U and memory. Next, prepare the OS: connect with SSH key authentication, update packages, and install the listed build dependencies for Substrate so compilation succeeds. Then secure the server: create a non-root user, disable root SSH login, and apply UFW rules that allow SSH and the P2P port while restricting RPC and WebSocket ports to trusted IPs. Finally, create a persistent base path for chain data, author a systemd service file with an ExecStart that points to your built binary and telemetry flags, enable the service, and validate with the systemctl and journalctl commands. Each step is a practical verification of deployment readiness.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Checklist

Deployment Checklist

Follow these verifiable tasks as you deploy.

1. Instance selection
Match role to resources and provision SSD-backed storage with room to grow.
2. SSH and OS updates
Use SSH keys, update packages, and install Substrate build tools before compiling.
3. Firewall rules
Allow SSH and P2P port; restrict RPC and WebSocket to trusted IP ranges.
4. systemd & monitoring
Install a service unit for automatic restarts and connect telemetry for observability.
Use this checklist during the hands-on activity. Each item is a verification point you can sign off on as the node moves from test to production.

screens.title: Choosing a Cloud Provider and Instance Type
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a cloud provider and instance type starts with defining the node's role. A full archival or serving node needs moderate C P U and memory, plus fast SSD storage provisioned for future chain growth. A validator needs stronger guarantees: more C P U, more R A M, and higher availability. Popular cloud vendors include AWS, GCP, DigitalOcean, and Linode, and the practical choice often depends on budget, region, and familiar tooling. For example, a simple full node can run comfortably on a DigitalOcean droplet with four gigabytes of memory and two virtual CPUs and an 80 gigabyte SSD, or on an AWS t3. medium. The key is not a single number but matching capacity to expected peers, RPC load, and storage growth. A common misconception is to optimize only for C P U; in blockchains, disk performance and available storage are equally critical because chain data grows over time. Your checklist: prefer SSDs, plan for extra disk headroom, and provision with a plan to resize or attach additional volumes later. Consider backup strategies for your chain data and how instance termination affects persistent volumes.

keyIdea.text: Pick CPU, RAM, and SSD capacity based on whether the node is full, archival, or a validator; prioritize SSD and disk headroom.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Instance Selection
Comparison

Full Node vs Validator

Compare resource priorities and availability expectations.

Full Node (example)
Moderate CPU (2 vCPU), 4–8 GB RAM, SSD storage. Good for testnets and serving peers.
Validator (example)
Higher CPU and RAM, strong network uptime, and higher availability commitments; consider dedicated or larger instances.
Storage priority
Prefer SSDs and provision more disk than you need. Blockchain storage grows over time and can become the bottleneck.
Concrete example
Example instance
A suggested starting point for a non-validator full node: DigitalOcean droplet with 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM and an 80 GB SSD, or AWS t3.medium or m5.large depending on availability.
Misconception check: CPU alone won't keep you in sync. If disk I/O stalls, the node falls behind regardless of CPU.
Key Takeaway

Choose SSD-backed storage with headroom, then match CPU and RAM to the node role and expected load.

screens.title: Provisioning and Initial SSH Connection
screens.narratorSegment: The first practical step after provisioning an instance is to establish a secure SSH connection and prepare the operating system. Use SSH key-based authentication rather than passwords; that means you create or reuse an SSH key pair and connect with your private key. Once connected, update system packages to ensure you have the latest security patches. On Debian and Ubuntu systems, the combined update and upgrade commands bring packages current. After this, install the Substrate build dependencies so you can compile on the instance if needed. In practice you will run commands to install build-essential, SSL headers, and the toolchain required by Rust/Cargo. A common pitfall is attempting to compile without these dependencies and then seeing long cryptic build failures. Another mistake is keeping the build output in a non-persistent home directory on ephemeral disks; create a dedicated, persistent base path for chain data. After initial setup, create a non-root user for day-to-day operations and restrict root SSH login. Provisioning and Initial SSH Connection means use ssh keys and update the os first. install build dependencies so compilation will succeed on the instance.. In practical terms, securely access your cloud instance and prepare the os. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › SSH & OS Prep
Process

Connect and prepare

Establish SSH access, update packages, and install needed build dependencies.

Terminal commands (example)
ssh -i ~/.ssh/your_key.pem root@YOUR_SERVER_IP

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

sudo apt install -y build-essential libssl-dev pkg-config clang curl git llvm
Replace placeholders with your key path and server IP. These commands update the OS and install common Substrate build tools.
Concrete scenario
You connect with your SSH key, run the update and install commands, then create a non-root user for running the node. This reduces the chance of accidental system changes and keeps service processes separate from administrative accounts.
Common mistake

Using password SSH or running the node as root increases security risk. Use key pairs and a dedicated user instead.

Key Takeaway

Secure SSH and install dependencies before you attempt to build or start the node to avoid build failures and exposure.

screens.title: SSH Key-Based Authentication and Server Hardening
screens.narratorSegment: SSH key-based authentication uses asymmetric cryptography to give you secure access without sending passwords over the network. You generate a private and public key pair locally, place the public key on the server, and keep the private key securely on your workstation. This approach reduces brute-force risk and is the industry standard for cloud servers. After enabling keys, create a non-root user and disable direct root login to limit the blast radius if credentials are exposed. Apply a firewall such as UFW and only allow ports you need: SSH and the P2P port must be reachable, while RPC and WebSocket endpoints should be restricted to trusted IP ranges. A common misconception is to open RPC publicly for convenience; this exposes administrative interfaces. Another pitfall is leaving default SSH ports unchanged without key authentication, which invites scanning. Always verify your firewall rules and test local RPC access before opening them externally. Ask yourself: who needs access and from which IPs? SSH Key-Based Authentication and Server Hardening means use ssh keys, non-root users, and a firewall to limit exposure of rpc and management interfaces.. In practical terms, principles for secure remote administration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › SSH & Hardening
Definition

SSH key authentication

Asymmetric keys replace passwords for secure, automated remote access.

Create a non-root user
Operate the node under a dedicated account to reduce risk from user-level mistakes.
Disable root login
Prevent direct root SSH access in your SSH server configuration to force sudo-based elevation.
Scenario & tips
After adding your public key to the server, attempt a connection and confirm you can sudo as the non-root user. Then update SSH daemon settings to disallow password authentication and root login. Finally, verify UFW rules to ensure only expected ports are accessible.
Common mistake

Opening RPC and WebSocket ports publicly for convenience. Restrict these to trusted IPs instead.

Pro tip

Keep a separate admin key and rotate keys periodically; document which IPs require RPC access.

screens.title: Firewall Configuration with UFW
screens.narratorSegment: A firewall is a simple and effective way to enforce network access rules on your cloud instance. The chapter demonstrates UFW, the uncomplicated firewall, as a practical tool on Debian and Ubuntu. The minimal set of rules you will apply allows SSH for administration and the Substrate peer-to-peer port so the node can connect to other peers. RPC and WebSocket endpoints should not be open broadly; instead allow them from trusted IP ranges or internal networks. The example commands enable UFW, allow SSH, allow the P2P port on its TCP port, and then add specific rules restricting the RPC and WebSocket ports to a trusted CIDR. After applying rules, always check UFW status to confirm the expected ports are permitted. A common troubleshooting step is to test RPC locally from the server to confirm the node is listening before changing external rules. Misconfiguring the firewall can block your SSH session, so plan admin access and a recovery path when altering remote firewall rules. Firewall Configuration with UFW means open the p2p port broadly, but restrict rpc and websocket endpoints to trusted ip ranges with ufw.. In practical terms, allow necessary traffic and restrict rpc/ws to trusted ips. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Firewall (UFW)
Process

UFW commands you will run

Enable UFW and add rules to allow SSH, P2P, and restricted RPC/WS access.

sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw allow ssh
sudo ufw allow 30333/tcp
sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 9933
sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 9944
sudo ufw status
Replace the CIDR with your trusted IP range. Confirm status before finishing.
Troubleshooting
If SSH is blocked by an incorrect rule, use your cloud provider's console to regain access, or schedule firewall changes during a maintenance window. Test RPC locally from the node before allowing remote access to ensure the service is listening correctly.
Common mistake

Opening RPC publicly makes your node accessible for control or data exfiltration. Always restrict RPC/WS to known IPs.

Key Takeaway

Apply minimal firewall rules: only the ports necessary for operation and only from trusted ranges where appropriate.

screens.title: Building the Substrate Node on the Server
screens.narratorSegment: Once the server is prepared and dependencies are installed, clone your Substrate node template and build it in release mode. Building on the server is straightforward but can take time; ensure you have necessary swap or memory available for the Rust toolchain. The chapter provides the canonical commands to clone the repository, change into the project and run the release build using Cargo. A key practical note: building in release mode produces the optimized binary you will run under systemd. If you have a precompiled binary, you can copy it onto the server instead, but make sure it targets the same distribution and architecture. A common misconception is that debug builds are fine for production; they lack the performance and optimizations required in an operational node. After the build completes, verify the binary path and size and plan a persistent base path for chain data that survives instance reboots or recreations. Building the Substrate Node on the Server means build the node in release mode on the server or transfer a compatible release binary; verify architecture and persistence.. In practical terms, clone the template and compile in release mode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Build
Code Walkthrough

Clone and compile

Use git to fetch the node template and then run a release build with Cargo.

git clone https://github.com/substrate-developer-hub/substrate-node-template.git
cd substrate-node-template
cargo build --release
This produces a release binary under target/release. Building may take time; ensure your instance has enough RAM and disk for the build artifacts.
Practical notes
If you prefer not to compile on the server, cross-compile or transfer an existing release binary matching the server architecture. Always verify the binary runs and that your chosen base path is persistent across restarts.
Misconception

Debug builds are acceptable for production. They are not; use release builds for performance and stability.

Key Takeaway

Build in release mode and confirm the binary path before authoring the systemd service file that will run it.

screens.title: Create Persistent Data Directory and Permissions
screens.narratorSegment: Chain data must be stored in a persistent location so that reboots, service restarts, or instance replacement do not lead to data loss. Create a dedicated data directory such as a folder under /var/lib and set ownership to the non-root user that will run the node. This directory is where you point the Substrate node's base-path argument. If your cloud instance uses ephemeral local storage, attach and mount a block volume and set appropriate permissions. The steps include creating the directory, setting ownership with chown, and verifying the non-root user can write to it. A common mistake is keeping chain data in a user's home directory which may be less clearly managed across provisioning workflows. Always ensure the service user has only the permissions it needs: full write to the base path, but not unnecessary system privileges. Finally, consider backup and snapshot strategies for this directory if you want additional recovery options. Create Persistent Data Directory and Permissions means put chain data on a persistent disk path owned by the service user so data survives reboots and instance changes.. In practical terms, ensure chain data is stored on a persistent, owned path. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Data Directory
Process

Create and assign a base path

Create /var/lib/substrate-node and set the service user as owner so the node can persist chain data.

sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/substrate-node
sudo chown -R your_user:your_user /var/lib/substrate-node
Replace your_user with the non-root account created earlier. Use mounted persistent volumes for long-lived data.
Best practice
Use a mounted block device for chain data rather than ephemeral local storage. This protects chain state across instance recreation and enables snapshots for recovery.
Key Takeaway

Ensure data is on a persistent volume and owned by the service user to survive reboots and to be managed by system backups.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › systemd Service
Example Service File
[Unit]
Description=Substrate Node
After=network.target

[Service]
User=your_user
Group=your_user
ExecStart=/home/your_user/substrate-node-template/target/release/node-template \
    --base-path /var/lib/substrate-node \
    --chain your_chain_spec.json \
    --name "My Production Node" \
    --rpc-external --ws-external \
    --rpc-cors all \
    --bootnodes /ip4/BOOTNODE_IP/tcp/30333/p2p/BOOTNODE_PEER_ID \
    --validator
Restart=always
RestartSec=10
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=substrate-node

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Replace placeholders with your user, chain spec, and bootnode details. The base-path should point to the persistent directory created earlier.
Enable and start
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable substrate-node.service
sudo systemctl start substrate-node.service
Key Takeaway

A systemd unit makes your node a managed service with restart policies and centralized logging via system journal.

screens.title: Verify Service Status and Logs
screens.narratorSegment: After starting the systemd service, verifying the node's status and streaming its logs is your first troubleshooting step. Use the service status command to check whether the unit is active and to see recent exit codes or errors. To view runtime logs in real time, stream the unit's journal entries. These logs show startup sequences, peer connections, syncing progress, and any binding errors related to network or RPC configuration. If RPC endpoints fail to bind externally, check that the service was started with the external flags and that firewall rules permit the traffic. A common debugging practice is to test the RPC endpoint locally on the server with a simple JSON-RPC call to system health to ensure the node is responsive before testing external connectivity. If the service repeatedly restarts, inspect journal entries for repeated crashes and consider resource constraints such as memory exhaustion or disk full conditions. These logs are the primary source of truth when a deployed node misbehaves. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to take a compiled Substrate node into the cloud and run it reliably. We'll cover the decisions that matter when choosing a provider and instance type, how to prepare a Linux server with secure access, why you should use a service manager rather than a terminal session, and what monitoring looks like for an operational node. You will see concrete command examples for an Ubuntu system, a defensible firewall setup, a persistent service file using the system's service manager, and options for telemetry and external monitoring. Knowing these steps matters because nodes need persistent connectivity, reliable restarts, and careful network controls to participate in a peer-to-peer blockchain safely. For example, a full node can run on a modest virtual machine with SSD storage while a validator requires greater availability and more powerful hardware. Keep a mental checklist: choose the right instance, lock down SSH, open only required ports, build in a persistent data path, run under systemd, and attach telemetry. As you proceed, ask: is my node resilient to reboots and restricted to the traffic I expect?

These learning objectives map to practical skills you'll use when deploying a Substrate node. First, you will learn to select an appropriate cloud provider and instance type by matching C P U, R A M, and SSD needs to the node role. For a full node that serves peers, modest virtual machines with solid-state storage are sufficient; for a validator you will place emphasis on availability and stronger hardware. Second, you will configure a Linux server environment: connect over SSH, update packages, and install the build dependencies required to compile a Substrate node. Third, you will implement secure SSH access and basic server hardening: use key-based authentication, create a non-root user, disable direct root login, and apply firewall rules that open only the P2P port broadly while restricting RPC and WebSocket to trusted IPs. Finally, you will set up the node as a persistent systemd service and monitor its health using journal logs and telemetry. Each objective is actionable and verifiable, so you'll be ready to run a resilient node in production.

This page turns objectives into a short checklist you can follow during deployment. Start by choosing a cloud provider and instance that fits your node role. If you run a simple full node, a small instance with solid-state drive and 4 gigabytes of memory often suffices; for validators prefer higher availability and more C P U and memory. Next, prepare the OS: connect with SSH key authentication, update packages, and install the listed build dependencies for Substrate so compilation succeeds. Then secure the server: create a non-root user, disable root SSH login, and apply UFW rules that allow SSH and the P2P port while restricting RPC and WebSocket ports to trusted IPs. Finally, create a persistent base path for chain data, author a systemd service file with an ExecStart that points to your built binary and telemetry flags, enable the service, and validate with the systemctl and journalctl commands. Each step is a practical verification of deployment readiness.

Choosing a cloud provider and instance type starts with defining the node's role. A full archival or serving node needs moderate C P U and memory, plus fast SSD storage provisioned for future chain growth. A validator needs stronger guarantees: more C P U, more R A M, and higher availability. Popular cloud vendors include AWS, GCP, DigitalOcean, and Linode, and the practical choice often depends on budget, region, and familiar tooling. For example, a simple full node can run comfortably on a DigitalOcean droplet with four gigabytes of memory and two virtual CPUs and an 80 gigabyte SSD, or on an AWS t3. medium. The key is not a single number but matching capacity to expected peers, RPC load, and storage growth. A common misconception is to optimize only for C P U; in blockchains, disk performance and available storage are equally critical because chain data grows over time. Your checklist: prefer SSDs, plan for extra disk headroom, and provision with a plan to resize or attach additional volumes later. Consider backup strategies for your chain data and how instance termination affects persistent volumes.

The first practical step after provisioning an instance is to establish a secure SSH connection and prepare the operating system. Use SSH key-based authentication rather than passwords; that means you create or reuse an SSH key pair and connect with your private key. Once connected, update system packages to ensure you have the latest security patches. On Debian and Ubuntu systems, the combined update and upgrade commands bring packages current. After this, install the Substrate build dependencies so you can compile on the instance if needed. In practice you will run commands to install build-essential, SSL headers, and the toolchain required by Rust/Cargo. A common pitfall is attempting to compile without these dependencies and then seeing long cryptic build failures. Another mistake is keeping the build output in a non-persistent home directory on ephemeral disks; create a dedicated, persistent base path for chain data. After initial setup, create a non-root user for day-to-day operations and restrict root SSH login. Provisioning and Initial SSH Connection means use ssh keys and update the os first. install build dependencies so compilation will succeed on the instance.. In practical terms, securely access your cloud instance and prepare the os. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SSH key-based authentication uses asymmetric cryptography to give you secure access without sending passwords over the network. You generate a private and public key pair locally, place the public key on the server, and keep the private key securely on your workstation. This approach reduces brute-force risk and is the industry standard for cloud servers. After enabling keys, create a non-root user and disable direct root login to limit the blast radius if credentials are exposed. Apply a firewall such as UFW and only allow ports you need: SSH and the P2P port must be reachable, while RPC and WebSocket endpoints should be restricted to trusted IP ranges. A common misconception is to open RPC publicly for convenience; this exposes administrative interfaces. Another pitfall is leaving default SSH ports unchanged without key authentication, which invites scanning. Always verify your firewall rules and test local RPC access before opening them externally. Ask yourself: who needs access and from which IPs? SSH Key-Based Authentication and Server Hardening means use ssh keys, non-root users, and a firewall to limit exposure of rpc and management interfaces.. In practical terms, principles for secure remote administration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A firewall is a simple and effective way to enforce network access rules on your cloud instance. The chapter demonstrates UFW, the uncomplicated firewall, as a practical tool on Debian and Ubuntu. The minimal set of rules you will apply allows SSH for administration and the Substrate peer-to-peer port so the node can connect to other peers. RPC and WebSocket endpoints should not be open broadly; instead allow them from trusted IP ranges or internal networks. The example commands enable UFW, allow SSH, allow the P2P port on its TCP port, and then add specific rules restricting the RPC and WebSocket ports to a trusted CIDR. After applying rules, always check UFW status to confirm the expected ports are permitted. A common troubleshooting step is to test RPC locally from the server to confirm the node is listening before changing external rules. Misconfiguring the firewall can block your SSH session, so plan admin access and a recovery path when altering remote firewall rules. Firewall Configuration with UFW means open the p2p port broadly, but restrict rpc and websocket endpoints to trusted ip ranges with ufw.. In practical terms, allow necessary traffic and restrict rpc/ws to trusted ips. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Once the server is prepared and dependencies are installed, clone your Substrate node template and build it in release mode. Building on the server is straightforward but can take time; ensure you have necessary swap or memory available for the Rust toolchain. The chapter provides the canonical commands to clone the repository, change into the project and run the release build using Cargo. A key practical note: building in release mode produces the optimized binary you will run under systemd. If you have a precompiled binary, you can copy it onto the server instead, but make sure it targets the same distribution and architecture. A common misconception is that debug builds are fine for production; they lack the performance and optimizations required in an operational node. After the build completes, verify the binary path and size and plan a persistent base path for chain data that survives instance reboots or recreations. Building the Substrate Node on the Server means build the node in release mode on the server or transfer a compatible release binary; verify architecture and persistence.. In practical terms, clone the template and compile in release mode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chain data must be stored in a persistent location so that reboots, service restarts, or instance replacement do not lead to data loss. Create a dedicated data directory such as a folder under /var/lib and set ownership to the non-root user that will run the node. This directory is where you point the Substrate node's base-path argument. If your cloud instance uses ephemeral local storage, attach and mount a block volume and set appropriate permissions. The steps include creating the directory, setting ownership with chown, and verifying the non-root user can write to it. A common mistake is keeping chain data in a user's home directory which may be less clearly managed across provisioning workflows. Always ensure the service user has only the permissions it needs: full write to the base path, but not unnecessary system privileges. Finally, consider backup and snapshot strategies for this directory if you want additional recovery options. Create Persistent Data Directory and Permissions means put chain data on a persistent disk path owned by the service user so data survives reboots and instance changes.. In practical terms, ensure chain data is stored on a persistent, owned path. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In production, run your Substrate node under the system service manager so it restarts automatically and integrates with system logs. The service file defines who runs the process, how to start it, restart behavior, and where data lives.
